item.title: Hermes Agent Memory: Two Small Files Beat a Vector Database
item.description: Models are stateless by design: every request independent, no continuity past the context window. Most frameworks bolt memory on afterward — a database to query, a window to stuff. Hermes inverts it: memory isn’t retrieved when needed but injected at every session start, curated, bounded, always active. Two files under 3,600 characters total.

item.title: PKM vs RAG vs Wiki vs Memory: Four Knowledge Jobs, Four Systems
item.description: PKM, wikis, RAG, and AI memory get discussed as rivals solving one problem. They don’t. PKM helps humans think, wikis preserve shared knowledge, RAG retrieves for machines, memory gives agents continuity. Mix them up and you get personal scratch in the wiki, sourceless-truth RAG, database-pretending memory, and automation-bloated PKM.

item.title: LLM Wiki: Compiled Knowledge RAG Cannot Replace
item.description: RAG became the default answer to giving models external knowledge: chunk, embed, retrieve at query time, generate. Useful — and overused. RAG optimizes access, not representation: it finds fragments but builds no stable domain understanding, retrieves context but never decides the canonical explanation. An LLM Wiki moves synthesis to ingest time, compiling sources into structured, linked, human-readable knowledge before any question arrives.

item.title: AI Assistant Architecture: LLM, Memory, Tools, Routing, Observability
item.description: A production assistant isn’t “an LLM with a prompt.” It’s a runtime turning intent into responses and actions through five layers: model, memory, tooling, routing, observability. That split matches provider APIs, MCP, self-hosted runtimes, and real systems alike — and every production disagreement eventually reduces to which context was visible, which tool executed, which model answered, which memory changed, and where the trace says time went.

item.title: Memory Systems in AI Assistants: Working, Structured, Retrieval
item.description: Memory turns assistants from reactive to persistent — and it’s where systems quietly rot. The old short-term/long-term split no longer covers modern agents. The working stack is three layers: working memory for the live run, structured state for durable truth, retrieval memory for supporting evidence — plus a consolidation policy that forgets as deliberately as it remembers.

item.title: Multi-Model System Design: The Right Model for the Right Task
item.description: Running a 70B model to summarize an email wastes money; running a 3B model to review production code courts disaster. Multi-model design isn’t about collecting models — it’s about architecture that puts the right model on the right task at the right time, with the simplest pattern that survives the constraints.

item.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns: Six Topologies and How Each Breaks
item.description: Single-agent systems peaked with bounded tasks and one prompt. Production moved on: organizations now run double-digit agent counts, and a large share of multi-agent pilots die within months of deployment. The killer isn’t the idea — it’s picking the wrong coordination topology, or the right one without knowing its failure modes.

item.title: Agent Skills vs MCP Servers: Where Should the Responsibility Live?
item.description: Agent skills and MCP servers are often presented as competing ways to extend an AI agent. That framing is wrong: a skill teaches the agent how to work, while an MCP server gives it governed access to live capabilities. The useful question is not which standard wins, but where each responsibility should live.
